title: Polio Threat Persists for India Despite Virus-Free Status, Experts Warn
excerpt: With wild poliovirus still endemic in Afghanistan and Pakistan, specialists say India's 2014 polio-free certification holds only if vaccination and surveillance do not slip.
body:
• India has reported no wild poliovirus case since January 13, 2011, and the WHO certified the South-East Asia Region polio-free on March 27, 2014 - but experts marking World Polio Day warned the risk of importation remains.
  • Wild poliovirus is still endemic only in Afghanistan and Pakistan; the Global Polio Eradication Initiative figures cited by HealthandMe put Afghanistan at 42 cases in 2026 as of October 21 and Pakistan at six.
  • The absolute risk explains the caution: the WHO says 1 in 200 infections leads to irreversible paralysis, and 5 to 10 per cent of those paralysed die when breathing muscles are immobilised.
  • For parents: polio has no cure, so do not skip doses because India is polio-free - complete the routine schedule and take children under five to pulse polio rounds when they are held.

Experts marking World Polio Day on October 24 warned that India's polio-free status does not remove the threat of the virus returning, because wild poliovirus continues to circulate in neighbouring Afghanistan and Pakistan. India reported its last case of wild poliovirus on January 13, 2011, and the World Health Organization declared its South-East Asia Region, which includes India, polio-free on March 27, 2014, HealthandMe reported. More than a decade later, specialists said maintaining that status still depends on vaccination coverage, surveillance and early detection.

"Just because a country is free from polio doesn't mean it is immune to the disease."

- Gulam A. Vahanvaty, Chairman, India National PolioPlus Committee, Rotary International

Where the virus still circulates

The latest figures from the Global Polio Eradication Initiative cited in the HealthandMe report show Afghanistan had reported 42 cases of wild poliovirus in 2026 as of October 21, while Pakistan had reported six. The two countries remain the only places where wild poliovirus is endemic. The WHO polio fact sheet makes the same structural point: as long as a single child remains infected, children in all countries are at risk, and failure to eradicate polio from the last strongholds could result in a global resurgence. Cases due to wild poliovirus have fallen by over 99 per cent since 1988, from an estimated 350,000 cases in more than 125 endemic countries to two endemic countries, the WHO said.

What the risk means in absolute terms

Polio mainly affects children under five. Most infections cause no obvious symptoms, but the WHO states that 1 in 200 infections - 0.5 per cent - leads to irreversible paralysis, usually in the legs, and that among those paralysed, 5 to 10 per cent die when their breathing muscles become immobilised. There is no cure; protection comes only from vaccination, given multiple times. India uses two vaccines, the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), given by injection, and the oral polio vaccine (OPV), given as drops, HealthandMe reported.

"Equally important is strong surveillance to identify suspected cases, monitor acute flaccid paralysis and detect any possible circulation of the virus at an early stage."

- Dr Aparna G, Consultant in Paediatrics and Neonatology, Rainbow Children's Hospital, Chennai

Surveillance is the second half of the defence

Dr Aparna said sustained immunisation is central to preventing the disease returning, and that the risk of the virus being reintroduced from neighbouring countries where it continues to circulate remains. Alongside vaccination, health authorities investigate acute flaccid paralysis - sudden-onset weakness or paralysis in children - and run environmental surveillance, testing sewage samples for poliovirus, which can detect circulation even when no case has been reported. Pulse polio rounds give extra OPV doses to all children below five in an area on a given day, repeated every year with the aim of 100 per cent coverage; those extra doses do not replace routine immunisation, and both approaches matter most for children who may have missed doses or live where access to care is poor.

What parents should do

The practical message for families in India and for diaspora parents travelling with young children is unchanged by the certificate: check the child's immunisation card, complete every scheduled dose, and use pulse polio rounds when they are announced rather than treating polio-free status as a reason to skip. Until transmission is interrupted everywhere, the experts' conclusion is that vaccination coverage, surveillance and international cooperation remain the conditions that keep India's 2014 certification true in practice, not just on paper.
